_**Gunstar Heroes**_[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-7) is a 1993 [run and gun video game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Run_and_gun_video_game "Run and gun video game") developed by [Treasure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treasure_(company) "Treasure (company)") and published by [Sega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega "Sega") for the [Sega Genesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Genesis "Sega Genesis"). It was Treasure's first developed video game. The premise is centered around a pair of characters, the Gunstars, in their efforts to stop an evil empire from recovering four powerful gems. The characters can fire guns and perform a series of acrobatic maneuvers to fight enemies across each stage. There are four weapons which can be combined with one another to create different shot types.

Development on _Gunstar Heroes_ began among a team of staff working at [Konami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konami "Konami") in 1991. Following an unwillingness of Konami to embrace their original game ideas, the team quit in 1992 and formed Treasure to see their project through. The team wanted to develop their game for the Genesis because of the system's powerful [Motorola 68000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motorola_68000 "Motorola 68000") microprocessor. [Sega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega "Sega") initially rejected their proposal, but later granted approval after they worked for Sega for several months on _[McDonald's Treasure Land Adventure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McDonald's\_Treasure\_Land\_Adventure "McDonald's Treasure Land Adventure")_ (1993). Treasure worked on both games in parallel, and released _Gunstar Heroes_ as their first game in 1993.

_Gunstar Heroes_ was a critical success, being praised for its frantic action and advanced graphics. It helped establish Treasure's place in the industry, and introduced numerous design conventions which would become characteristic of their later work such as large bosses and a unique sense of humor. It was re-released several times, including dedicated ports to the [Game Gear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Gear "Game Gear") and [Nintendo 3DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_3DS "Nintendo 3DS"), and received [a sequel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Super_Heroes "Gunstar Super Heroes") on the [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance"). In retrospect, it is considered one of the best action games of the [16-bit era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_generation_of_video_game_consoles "Fourth generation of video game consoles"), and one of the [best video games of all time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_video_games_considered_the_best "List of video games considered the best") by several publications.

## Gameplay

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gunstar_Heroes&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Gameplay")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/0/00/Gunstar_Heroes_screenshot.png/250px-Gunstar_Heroes_screenshot.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gunstar_Heroes_screenshot.png)

The player runs to the right as they fire the machine gun.

_Gunstar Heroes_ is a [run and gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Run_and_gun_(video_game) "Run and gun (video game)") game which is played from a [side-scrolling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Side-scrolling_video_game "Side-scrolling video game") perspective similar to [_Contra_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contra_(series) "Contra (series)").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-nwrr-8) The game can be played in [single-player](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single-player_video_game "Single-player video game"), or [cooperatively](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooperative_video_game "Cooperative video game") with a partner. The players take on the role of Gunstar Red and Gunstar Blue as they battle with an evil empire for control over a set of powerful gems.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-tar-9) The game features seven stages, of which the first four can be played in any order.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-tar-9) The stage formats vary. While some feature a left-to-right format, others include the player riding in a mine cart along walls, fighting enemies on a helicopter, or playing a board game.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-tar-9)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-usgr-10) Completing a level grants the player an extension to their maximum health, known as vitality in the game.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-tar-9)

When starting the game, the player can choose either a free or fixed firing stance; the free stance allows the player to move in the direction they are firing, while the fixed stance immobilizes the character when shooting.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-usgr-10) The player also has a choice of starting weapon. There are four shot types in the game: a homing shot, lightning blaster, flamethrower, and machine gun. Every weapon has its strengths and weaknesses, and can be swapped with others from item drops.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:26-11) The weapons can be combined with each other to produce unique shot types. For example, the homing shot can be combined with the machine gun to add a homing effect to the latter, or two lightning shots can be combined to create a more powerful lightning gun.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:26-11) In addition to firing their weapon, the player characters can perform a series of acrobatic maneuvers including jumping, sliding, and grabbing and throwing enemies.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-tar-9)

## Development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gunstar_Heroes&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Development")]

In 1991, several [Konami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konami "Konami") employees led by programmer Masato Maegawa began holding planning sessions at coffee shops for an original game.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:4-12)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:1-13) They were establishing early concepts for an action shooting game, a genre they were familiar with.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:1-13) They pitched their idea to Konami, but were told it would not sell and it was rejected.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:0-14) Maegawa and his team were growing frustrated with the industry's reliance on sequels to established franchises and console conversions of arcade games to generate revenue.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:0-14) They felt Konami had fallen into this pattern as a large company, growing reliant on sequels in their _[Castlevania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castlevania "Castlevania")_ and _[Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List\_of\_Teenage\_Mutant\_Ninja\_Turtles\_video\_games "List of Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles video games")_ series.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:0-14) Maegawa and his team felt consumers wanted original games,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:0-14) and so in 1992, they left Konami and established [Treasure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treasure_(company) "Treasure (company)") to continue development on their unique game.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-works4-15)

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/26/Sega-Genesis-Mod1-Set.png/250px-Sega-Genesis-Mod1-Set.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sega-Genesis-Mod1-Set.png)

Treasure believed the [Motorola 68000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motorola_68000 "Motorola 68000") microprocessor in the [Sega Genesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Genesis "Sega Genesis") was best suited for the action games they wanted to make.

Treasure wanted to develop their game for the [Sega Genesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Genesis "Sega Genesis").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:0-14) Maegawa liked the platform because of its [Motorola 68000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motorola_68000 "Motorola 68000") microprocessor, which he felt was easier to program for than the [Super NES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_NES "Super NES"), and more powerful.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:0-14) The team decided to approach Sega for a publishing contract.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:4-12) When they presented their design documents to Sega, they were not granted approval because they lacked a proven track record.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:1-13) Instead, Sega contracted Treasure to develop _[McDonald's Treasure Land Adventure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McDonald's\_Treasure\_Land\_Adventure "McDonald's Treasure Land Adventure")_ (1993).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:1-13) Several months into development, they were granted approval to work on their game.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:1-13) They were initially using the working title _Lunatic Gunstar_, thinking "Lunatic" was a good description of the stimulating action.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:4-12) Sega of America felt the word held a negative connotation, so rejected it.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:1-13) The team also considered _Blade Gunner_, in homage to _[Blade Runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blade\_Runner "Blade Runner")_, but this was also rejected due to copyright restrictions.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:1-13) Sega of America eventually suggested the word "Heroes", so _Gunstar Heroes_ became the final title.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:1-13)

Treasure consisted of around 18 people, most being programmers from Konami.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:0-14) The staff was split in half to work on both _Gunstar Heroes_ and _McDonald's Treasure Land Adventure_ in parallel.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:1-13)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:0-14) The core team behind _Gunstar Heroes_ consisted of six people: two programmers, two graphic designers, and two sound programmers.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:0-14) The staff (known by their nicknames) was composed of main programmer Yaiman, enemy and boss programmer Nami, graphic designers Han and Iuchi, composer Non, and sound effects programmer Murata.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:4-12) The role of game designer did not exist within Treasure. All game design and planning was undertaken by everyone involved.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-works4-15) The team felt they had more freedom working under Sega than Konami.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:0-14) Maegawa got approval to add a Treasure logo when the game booted, which he felt was a rare opportunity for developers to receive during that era.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:1-13)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/2/23/GunstarHeroes_SevenForce.gif/250px-GunstarHeroes_SevenForce.gif?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GunstarHeroes_SevenForce.gif)

The Genesis's processor made multi-limbed bosses like "Seven Force" possible.

Development of _Gunstar Heroes_ lasted around nine to ten months.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:4-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:0-14) It was the team's first experience programming for the Genesis, having come off of programming for the Super NES at Konami.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:1-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-works4-15) Programmers Mitsuru Yaida and Hideyuki Suganami previously programmed _[Contra III: The Alien Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contra\_III:\_The\_Alien\_Wars "Contra III: The Alien Wars")_ (1992) for the Super NES at Konami.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-euroretrospec-16) The team felt the Genesis's processor was more powerful, capable, and friendly to experimentation than other consoles. This led them to consider it more suited for action games and the sophisticated graphical effects they were looking to create.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:1-13)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:0-14)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-works4-15) The team implemented heavy visual effects in an exercise in design experimentation (not an effort to push the hardware).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-works4-15) Some of that experimenting was done with the system's [sprite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sprite_(computer_graphics) "Sprite (computer graphics)") rotation and scaling capabilities, which evoked a sense of depth.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:4-12)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:1-13)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:0-14) The Genesis had its limitations however, as it could only display 64 colors on-screen at once.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:0-14) The team placed extra effort on coloring to compensate.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-works4-15) Early backgrounds were drawn with a 16 color palette, but they looked desolate, so ultimately two palettes with 32 colors were used.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:4-12) The team also used programming tricks to make the scenery appear like three to four layers were present, even though the Genesis only supports two.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:0-14)

The team approached _Gunstar Heroes_ with an "anything goes" concept, that led to many ambitious ideas being implemented into the final game.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:4-12)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:1-13) One such concept was the weapon combination mechanic, which was conceived in the early planning stages.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-works4-15) They experimented with weapon attributes until the end of development,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-works4-15) and designed the game so players would continue discovering new weapons and devise unique ways to complete stages.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:4-12) The processor also made articulated multi-limb enemies possible, like the boss "Seven Force", which was programmed by Nami along with all other bosses.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:1-13) Since moving around large sprites was difficult due to limited [video RAM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_RAM_(dual-ported_DRAM) "Video RAM (dual-ported DRAM)"), Seven Force was built by combining circles and squares to make one large character.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:1-13) Maegawa claims the game would not have worked on the Super NES because the boss animations required expanded computing power.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:0-14) The standard enemy characters, designed by Han, were drawn on the screen by combining a top and bottom sprite, allowing for more animation patterns with lower memory usage.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:1-13) Han was inspired by the game _[Mazin Saga: Mutant Fighter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mazin\_Saga:\_Mutant\_Fighter "Mazin Saga: Mutant Fighter")_ (1993) to program the enemies manually rather than with mathematical algorithms.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-B!MD49-17) The game was 16 [megabits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megabit "Megabit"), but compressed to fit under 8.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:0-14)

## Release

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gunstar_Heroes&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Release")]

Although _McDonald's Treasure Land Adventure_ was completed beforehand, Treasure decided to wait and release _Gunstar Heroes_ first because they wanted their debut to be an original game.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:1-13) It was nearly rejected for an American release by Sega of America, only being approved by Mac Senour, the last producer in the reviewing queue after 12 others rejected it. Senour believed the other producers dismissed the game because its small character sprites contrasted with the more popular large sprites at the time. Senour did ask Treasure to change one boss character because it looked too similar to [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:2-18)

_Gunstar Heroes_ was released in Japan on September 10, 1993,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-vc-2) and released in the West the same month.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:4-12) Sega underestimated demand in Japan where their initial shipment was only 10,000 units.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:9-19) Meanwhile, Sega of America also ordered a small initial print run, as they were not typically confident in games from Sega of Japan.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:2-18) The game was not heavily promoted and spread through speech.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:3-20)_[GameFan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameFan "GameFan")_ particularly enjoyed the game and published the first English interview with Maegawa.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:3-20) The game shipped around 70,000 copies in Japan, and 200,000 overseas.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:9-19) An arcade version was also released for the [Sega Mega-Play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Mega_Play "Sega Mega Play") arcade board.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:1-13)

### Ports and re-releases

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gunstar_Heroes&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Ports and re-releases")]

A modified version was released for Sega's [Mega-Play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Mega_Play "Sega Mega Play") arcade hardware in 1994. Changes include multiple lives being given per credit (as opposed to a single life in the console version), a 10-second timer which forces the player to make a decision when appropriate, and [continuous play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continue_(video_gaming) "Continue (video gaming)") by inserting additional credits.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

A [Game Gear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Gear "Game Gear") port was developed by [M2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M2_(game_developer) "M2 (game developer)"). Sega asked M2 if they wanted to make a Game Gear game after being impressed by their _[Gauntlet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauntlet\_IV "Gauntlet IV")_ port for the Genesis. M2 wanted to port _[The Cliffhanger: Edward Randy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Cliffhanger:\_Edward\_Randy "The Cliffhanger: Edward Randy")_, but they were ultimately handed _Gunstar Heroes_. Since the Genesis version pushed hardware limitations, a Game Gear port was difficult.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:5-21) The port had some changes, such as the Dice Palace being removed, and it ran at lower frame rate.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:4-12) It was released on March 24, 1995.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-22)

Sega released _Gunstar Heroes Treasure Box_ in 2006 in Japan, a compilation of Treasure games for the [PlayStation 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_2 "PlayStation 2") as part of their _[Sega Ages 2500](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega\_Ages "Sega Ages")_ series.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:6-23) Included on the compilation were _Gunstar Heroes_, _[Dynamite Headdy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamite\_Headdy "Dynamite Headdy")_ (1994), and _[Alien Soldier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alien\_Soldier "Alien Soldier")_ (1995).[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:4-12)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:6-23) The games are run through an emulator and include display options for filters and resolutions. The Japanese and international versions were included, along with the Game Gear ports of _Gunstar Heroes_ and _Dynamite Headdy_, and a Genesis prototype of _Gunstar Heroes_.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-24) A gallery is included with scans of the original instruction manuals, concept illustrations, and design documents.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:8-25) The compilation was released digitally on the [PlayStation Store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_Store "PlayStation Store") in 2012.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:8-25)

The game was ported by M2 to the [Nintendo 3DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_3DS "Nintendo 3DS") in 2015 as part of Sega's line of _[3D Classics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega\_3D\_Reprint\_Archives "Sega 3D Reprint Archives")_.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:7-26)_Gunstar Heroes_ was originally not considered for the series because converting the game's backgrounds into a layered 3D effect was thought to be impossible, but these perceived problems were later overcome.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-27) In addition to supporting [stereoscopic 3D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereoscopic_3d "Stereoscopic 3d"), the game features two new modes. "Gunslinger" mode starts the player with a full arsenal of every weapon type and grants the ability to change shot stance at any time. "Mega Life" mode starts the player with double the normal amount of health.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-28) The game also supports local cooperative play and includes both the Japanese and international versions.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:7-26)

_Gunstar Heroes_ has also been released on the [Xbox 360](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_360 "Xbox 360"),[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-29)[PlayStation 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_3 "PlayStation 3"),[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-30)[Wii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii "Wii") via [Virtual Console](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_Console "Virtual Console"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:26-11) and [Windows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-31) A [Sega Forever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Forever "Sega Forever") version for mobile devices was released in 2017.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-tar-9) The game was again released via the [Nintendo Classics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Classics "Nintendo Classics") service in 2021.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-32)

_Gunstar Heroes_ achieved greater recognition than Treasure anticipated.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:1-13)_[Electronic Gaming Monthly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic\_Gaming\_Monthly "Electronic Gaming Monthly")_ called it their "Game of the Month",[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-egmr-34) and the game placed first in _[Beep! Mega Drive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gemaga "Gemaga")_'s reader rankings in Japan.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:1-13)_GameFan_ deemed it their "Game of the Year"[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-gfanaward-42) and called it a new benchmark for action games.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-gfanr-44)_[Mean Machines Sega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean\_Machines\_Sega "Mean Machines Sega")_ wrote that _Gunstar Heroes_ was setting a new standard for action games on the Genesis, calling it "a stunning title both in appearance and the gameplay it offers."[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-mmsr-39)_Electronic Gaming Monthly_ agreed, with a critic calling it "one of the most intense games I've seen on the home video game scene."[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-egmr-34) Both _[Sega Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega\_Magazine "Sega Magazine")_ and _[Sega Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega\_Force "Sega Force")_ felt the game was a must-buy for Genesis owners.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-smagr-41)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-sforcer-40)

The game was commended for its fast and furious action.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-egmr-34)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-CVG-4)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-sforcer-40)_Electronic Gaming Monthly_ called it "one of the most intense carts to date [...] nonstop intensity from beginning to end."[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-egmr-34)_Mean Machines Sega_ agreed, praising the variety in level design and the "frantic, high-density blasting mayhem."[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-mmsr-39)_Sega Force_ believed the game's variety prevented it from falling into monotony, and instead, reinvigorated the platform genre.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-sforcer-40)_[Computer and Video Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer\_and\_Video\_Games "Computer and Video Games")_ agreed, feeling gameplay customization options kept it interesting and original.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-CVG-4) Some critics praised the player characters' acrobatics and attack maneuvers for adding excitement.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-mmsr-39)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-gpror-38)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-edger-33)_[GamePro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GamePro "GamePro")_ called _Gunstar Heroes_ "chaos in a cart" with "murderous action, excellent controls, and imaginative game design."[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-gpror-38) The two-player cooperative mode was praised,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-egmr-34)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-edger-33) though some felt there was too much clutter on the screen to tell the player characters apart.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-CVG-4)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-gpror-38)

The graphics were highlighted by several critics, with _GamePro_ calling it "an assault on your senses."[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-gpror-38)_Mean Machines Sega_ felt the sprite rotating and scaling overshadowed the abilities of the Super NES.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-mmsr-39)_Sega Magazine_ also liked the sprite scaling, and highlighted its use on the boss "Seven Force".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-smagr-41) Other critics also felt the bosses were well animated and designed,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-egmr-34)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-sforcer-40)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-edger-33) with some extending their comments to the player characters' animations as well.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-mmsr-39)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-sforcer-40)_Computer and Video Games_ commended the graphical explosion effects,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-CVG-4) with other critics praising the sound effects they were paired with for enhancing the game's atmosphere.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-sforcer-40)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-egmr-34)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-gpror-38) A critic from _Electronic Gaming Monthly_ called it "one of the best looking carts I've seen from Sega in a while."[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-egmr-34)

### Ports

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gunstar_Heroes&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Ports")]

Critics lauded the Game Gear port as a great 8-bit conversion.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-mmsgg-45)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-gfangg-46)_GameFan_ felt it was graphically advanced for a Game Gear game.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-gfangg-46)_Mean Machines Sega_ agreed, thinking that the graphics remained true to the 16-bit original despite greater system limitations.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-mmsgg-45) The 3DS version was praised for the added options and enhancements, with _[USgamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USGamer "USGamer")_ and _Nintendo World Report_ calling it the best version of the game.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-nwrr-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-usgr-10) The mobile version was criticized for being difficult to play with touch controls.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-tar-9)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gunstar_Heroes&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Legacy")]

_Gunstar Heroes_ was listed as one of the best games ever made by several publications.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-47)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-48)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-49)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-EGM100-50)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-51)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-52) Critics have called it a "classic" of the 16-bit era,[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:7-26)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-nwrr-8) with _IGN_ writing that its pace and speed was "nearly unrivaled" at the time.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:26-11) Others called it one of the best Genesis games.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-nwrr-8)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:27-53)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:28-54)_[Electronic Gaming Monthly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic\_Gaming\_Monthly "Electronic Gaming Monthly")_ called it "one of the best two-player games ever made."[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-EGM100-50)_USgamer_ wrote that its chaotic and brash nature made it the "quintessential classic-era Sega game" in contrast to the more gentle offerings from [Nintendo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo "Nintendo").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-usgr-10)_Nintendo World Report_ called it "an incredible accomplishment, both creatively and technically" for the Genesis.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-nwrr-8) Both _TouchArcade_ and _GameSpy_ deemed it one of the best side-scrolling action games ever made.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-tar-9)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:27-53)

Being Treasure's debut game, _Gunstar Heroes_ helped establish their reputation in the industry.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:4-12)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:23-55)_Retro Gamer_ said the game "blew open the state of 2D platform-shooters."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:4-12) Developers at the time borrowed inspiration for titles like _[Vectorman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vectorman "Vectorman")_ (1995) and _[Shinobi III: Return of the Ninja Master](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinobi\_III:\_Return\_of\_the\_Ninja\_Master "Shinobi III: Return of the Ninja Master")_ (1993).[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-56)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-57) Treasure also started building a following of loyal hardcore fans,[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-58) which _USgamer_ felt was earned by "a sense of integrity to Treasure's work you don't often see in games of that era."[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:23-55)_[1UP.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1Up.com "1Up.com")_ wrote that between _Gunstar Heroes_ and their other Genesis games, Treasure earned a reputation as a "master of hardcore action gaming."[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:3-20) Many of the design conventions Treasure used in _Gunstar Heroes_ would return and became characteristic of their later work, such as a quirky sense of humor and action taken to a level of absurdity.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:3-20) A sequel was released for the Game Boy Advance in 2005, _[Gunstar Super Heroes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar\_Super\_Heroes "Gunstar Super Heroes")_.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar_Heroes#cite_note-:4-12)

**Treasure Co., Ltd.**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-1) is a Japanese [video game developer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_developer "Video game developer") based in [Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo "Tokyo") known for its [action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_game "Action game"), [platform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platform_game "Platform game"), and [shoot 'em up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoot_'em_up "Shoot 'em up") games. The company was founded in 1992 by former [Konami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konami "Konami") employees seeking to explore original game concepts and free themselves from Konami's reliance on sequels. Their first game, _[Gunstar Heroes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar\_Heroes "Gunstar Heroes")_ (1993) on the [Sega Genesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Genesis "Sega Genesis"), was a critical success and established a creative and action-oriented design style that would continue to characterize its output. Treasure's philosophy in game development has always been to make games they enjoy, not necessarily those that have the greatest commercial viability.

Treasure grew a [cult following](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult_following "Cult following") for its action games developed during the 1990s, and though initially exclusive to [Sega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega "Sega") platforms, the studio expanded to other platforms in 1997. The company earned recognition from critics, being called one of the best Japanese indie studios and 2D game developers. The company's output decreased in the 2010s, with its most recent release being _Gaist Crusher God_ in 2014.

graduating.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-works4-2) At Konami, Maegawa and associates that would later establish Treasure worked on a variety of games including arcade titles [_The Simpsons_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Simpsons_(video_game) "The Simpsons (video game)") (1991) and _[Bucky O'Hare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bucky\_O'Hare\_(arcade\_game) "Bucky O'Hare (arcade game)")_ (1992), and [Super NES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Nintendo_Entertainment_System "Super Nintendo Entertainment System") games _[Super Castlevania Alien Wars")_ (1992), and _[Axelay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axelay "Axelay")_ (1992).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:0-3)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-EDGE44-4) In 1991, Maegawa and several other Konami employees began planning an original game that would become _[Gunstar Heroes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar\_Heroes "Gunstar Heroes")_ (1993)_,_[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:4-5)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:12-6) but their concept was rejected by Konami.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:0-3) Maegawa and his team were growing frustrated with Konami's growing reliance on sequels to established franchises such as its _[Castlevania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castlevania "Castlevania")_ and _[Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List\_of\_Teenage\_Mutant\_Ninja\_Turtles\_video\_games "List of Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles video games")_ series.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:0-3) The team felt consumers wanted original games,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:0-3) and so they left Konami in 1992 to establish Treasure and continue development on _Gunstar Heroes_.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-works4-2)

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/26/Sega-Genesis-Mod1-Set.png/250px-Sega-Genesis-Mod1-Set.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sega-Genesis-Mod1-Set.png)

In its first years, Treasure developed video games for the [Sega Genesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Genesis "Sega Genesis").

Treasure was founded on June 19, 1992;[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-7) the company name came from wanting to be a "treasure" to the industry.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:0-3) Around the time of founding, the company had just over ten people.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:6-8) Even though most of the staff made games for the Super NES at Konami, they wanted to develop _Gunstar Heroes_ for the [Sega Genesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Genesis "Sega Genesis") because the system's [Motorola 68000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motorola_68000 "Motorola 68000") microprocessor was necessary for the visuals and gameplay they were striving for.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:0-3) Treasure approached [Sega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega "Sega") for a publishing contract.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:4-5) At first, they were not granted approval because they lacked a track record, but Sega instead contracted them to develop _[McDonald's Treasure Land Adventure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McDonald's\_Treasure\_Land\_Adventure "McDonald's Treasure Land Adventure")_ (1993).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:12-6) Several months into development, they were granted approval to work on _Gunstar Heroes_.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:12-6) Treasure staff was split into two teams to work on both games in parallel.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:0-3)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:12-6) They had a staff of around 18 people at the time, most being ex-Konami programmers.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:0-3) The staff felt they had more freedom working under Sega than Konami.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:0-3)

_McDonald's Treasure Land Adventure_ was completed first, but Treasure decided to finish and release _Gunstar Heroes_ first because they wanted their debut to be an original game.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:12-6) North American magazine _[GameFan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameFan "GameFan")_ were enthralled with the game and secured the first English language interview with Treasure that year.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:1-9)_McDonald's Treasure Land Adventure_ was released next, initiating a trend for Treasure of developing games based on licensed properties. As a small studio, Treasure required the revenue from licensed games to develop original projects.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:1-9) Treasure continued to develop games for the Genesis for the remainder of the 16-bit era because of the system's smooth sprite movement, and grew a following among Sega fans.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:1-9)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:2-10) After _Gunstar Heroes_, Treasure was divided into four teams to develop (in order of release): platformer _[Dynamite Headdy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamite\_Headdy "Dynamite Headdy")_ (1994), fighting game _[Yu Yu Hakusho Makyō Tōitsusen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yu\_Yu\_Hakusho\_Maky%C5%8D\_T%C5%8Ditsusen "Yu Yu Hakusho Makyō Tōitsusen")_ (1994), run and gun _[Alien Soldier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alien\_Soldier "Alien Soldier")_ (1995), and action-adventure _[Light Crusader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light\_Crusader "Light Crusader")_ (1995).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:12-6) The variety among these games illustrated unevenness and unpredictability in Treasure's output that would become characteristic of them.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:1-9)

#### 32-bit era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Treasure_(company)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 32-bit era")]

In 1994, Sega introduced the [Sega Saturn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Saturn "Sega Saturn") technology to Treasure. Treasure were impressed with the system's ability to handle a large number of sprites. They also knew their fan base consisted entirely of Sega gamers, so as the [32-bit era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifth_generation_of_video_game_consoles "Fifth generation of video game consoles") began, they moved development to the Saturn.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:2-10) Even though the Saturn was capable of 3D graphics, they continued to develop 2D games because they had built up 2D sprite know-how. Competition from 3D games did not concern them.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:2-10) First on Saturn was _[Guardian Heroes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guardian\_Heroes "Guardian Heroes")_ (1996), a beat 'em up that combines elements from fighting games and RPGs.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:1-9) Treasure worked on their next two releases concurrently, side-scrolling platformers _[Mischief Makers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mischief\_Makers "Mischief Makers")_ (1997) and _[Silhouette Mirage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silhouette\_Mirage "Silhouette Mirage")_ (1997).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:1-9)_Mischief Makers_ was released on the [Nintendo 64](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_64 "Nintendo 64") and published by [Enix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enix "Enix"), Treasure's first game published by a company other than Sega and released on non-Sega hardware.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:1-9) Treasure chose to develop for the Nintendo 64 because they were interested in the hardware's capabilities.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-EDGE44-4) Enix had heard of Treasure's reputation for action games and requested to publish for them in the past, but it was not until Treasure was developing for a non-Sega platform that they sought Enix's cooperation.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-EDGE44-4)_Mischief Makers_ was followed by _Silhouette Mirage_, which was initially released on the Saturn then ported to the [PlayStation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_(console) "PlayStation (console)") in 1998.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:1-9)

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/OldTreasureHQ.jpg/250px-OldTreasureHQ.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:OldTreasureHQ.jpg)

Treasure's headquarters in [Nakano, Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nakano,_Tokyo "Nakano, Tokyo") from the late 1990s[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-12) to early 2010s[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-16) (photographed in 2019)

In 1998, Treasure released its first arcade game, the shoot 'em up _[Radiant Silvergun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiant\_Silvergun "Radiant Silvergun")_. Treasure had been hesitant to develop an arcade game for years because of concerns with their commercial viability, but the staff felt _Radiant Silvergun_ had potential and it was eager to develop it.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:22-17) The game was ported to the Saturn later that year.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:1-9) Enix published Treasure's next game for the PlayStation, fighting game _[Rakugaki Showtime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rakugaki\_Showtime "Rakugaki Showtime")_ (1999), but had to pull it from shelves shortly after release because of a lawsuit filed against them.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:1-9)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:3-13) This was followed by the [multidirectional shooter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoot_'em_up#Multidirectional_shooter "Shoot 'em up")_[Bangai-O](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangai-O "Bangai-O")_ (1999) which received a limited release on the Nintendo 64, but was later modified and re-released for the Dreamcast.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:1-9) By 1999, most of the founding Treasure staff were still with the company.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:10-18)

### Transition to licensed games (2000s)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Treasure_(company)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Transition to licensed games (2000s)")]

Treasure began the 2000s with some early troubles.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:1-9)_[Gun Beat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gun\_Beat "Gun Beat")_, a racing game they were developing for Sega's [NAOMI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SEGA_NAOMI "SEGA NAOMI") arcade platform, was canceled with little explanation.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:5-19) Also, _[Silpheed: The Lost Planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silpheed:\_The\_Lost\_Planet "Silpheed: The Lost Planet")_ (2000) and _[Stretch Panic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stretch\_Panic "Stretch Panic")_ (2001) for the PlayStation 2 both weren't received very well.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:1-9)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:3-13) Despite these hiccups, Treasure did find success with _[Sin and Punishment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sin\_and\_Punishment "Sin and Punishment")_ (2000),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:1-9) a [rail shooter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_shooter "Rail shooter") co-developed with Nintendo for the Nintendo 64 and later released on the [iQue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IQue "IQue") in China.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-20) The game was not released in western territories but grew a cult following among [import gamers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_importing_in_video_games "Parallel importing in video games").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:11-21) While _Sin and Punishment_ was still in development, Treasure started development on a spiritual sequel to _Radiant Silvergun_ titled _[Ikaruga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ikaruga "Ikaruga")_ (2001).[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-shump2001-22) The arcade shooter was co-developed with G.rev,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:3-13) and ported to the [Dreamcast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dreamcast "Dreamcast") and saw a worldwide release on the [GameCube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube "GameCube").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:1-9)

Treasure next embarked on a series of licensed projects.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:1-9) Two of these were based on the _[Tiny Toon Adventures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiny\_Toon\_Adventures "Tiny Toon Adventures")_ franchise, _[Tiny Toon Adventures: Buster's Bad Dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiny\_Toon\_Adventures:\_Buster's\_Bad\_Dream "Tiny Toon Adventures: Buster's Bad Dream")_ (2002) for the [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance") and the unreleased _[Tiny Toon Adventures: Defenders of the Universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiny\_Toon\_Adventures:\_Defenders\_of\_the\_Universe "Tiny Toon Adventures: Defenders of the Universe")_ for the PlayStation 2.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:1-9) Other licensed games during this period included Game Boy Advance games _[Hajime no Ippo: The Fighting!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajime\_no\_Ippo#Video\_games "Hajime no Ippo")_ (2003) and _[Astro Boy: Omega Factor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astro\_Boy:\_Omega\_Factor "Astro Boy: Omega Factor")_ (2003), as well as GameCube games _[Wario World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wario\_World "Wario World")_ (2003) and _Dragon Drive: D-Masters Shot_ (2003).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:1-9)_Astro Boy: Omega Factor_ was co-developed with Hitmaker[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-23) and was critically praised for returning to Treasure's classic side-scrolling action style that had been missing from its recent output.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:1-9)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:3-13) Their next game was _[Gradius V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gradius\_V "Gradius V")_ (2004) which like _Ikaruga_ before it, was co-developed with [G.rev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G.rev "G.rev").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:3-13) The companies worked under contract for Konami, and the game helped cement Treasure's return to critical successes following a slew of mediocre licensed games.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:1-9)

Treasure developed sequels on the Game Boy Advance for their earlier successes, _[Advance Guardian Heroes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advance\_Guardian\_Heroes "Advance Guardian Heroes")_ (2004) and _[Gunstar Super Heroes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunstar\_Super\_Heroes "Gunstar Super Heroes")_ (2005).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:1-9) Treasure followed this with a series of licensed _[Bleach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bleach\_(manga) "Bleach (manga)")_ games for the [Nintendo DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_DS "Nintendo DS").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:3-13) Maegawa explained that his company experiences challenges in developing games based on licensed properties like _Bleach_, saying that the staff wants to be original but cannot detract too far from the source material and risk disappointing fans.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:7-24) By 2009, the company had 20-30 employees.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:7-24)

### Output decline (2010s)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Treasure_(company)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Output decline (2010s)")]

The number of employees at Treasure had dropped to 16 by 2011.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:3-13) In a 2011 interview, Maegawa explained that Treasure now uses [middleware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleware "Middleware") to develop games, no longer using custom programming to push the hardware to their maximum levels.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:3-13) The company was also putting an increased focus on rereleasing their back catalog as downloadable games on the [Virtual Console](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_Console "Virtual Console"), [PlayStation Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PlayStation_Network "PlayStation Network"), and [Xbox Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_Live "Xbox Live").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:3-13) Treasure has not released any new games since 2014 apart from re-releases of games like _Ikaruga_.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:9-25)

### 2020s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Treasure_(company)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 2020s")]

On June 19, 2022, its 30th anniversary, Treasure announced it was working on a "highly requested" game.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-VGCHighlyRequested-26) Shortly afterwards, it re-released _Radiant Silvergun_ for the Nintendo Switch.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-VGCHighlyRequested2-27) They had less than 10 staff by 2022.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-VGCHighlyRequested-26)

## Staff and design philosophy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Treasure_(company)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Staff and design philosophy")]

Treasure does not have a rigid hierarchy.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:6-8)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:3-13) Maegawa explained that Treasure operates differently from other companies by not assigning lead designers. While a project leader may create a project plan, most of the game design is done collaboratively between the programmers and artists.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:6-8) Most permanent employees and part-time contractors drift in and out of projects as required.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:3-13) Some individuals have been important figures in Treasure's history:[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:3-13)

*   Masato Maegawa – Founder, company president, and lead producer on all games.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:6-8) He was programmer for some of the company's Genesis games.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:3-13)
*   Hideyuki Suganami – Programmer on _Gunstar Heroes_, _Alien Soldier_, _Mischief Makers_, and _Sin and Punishment_. Suganami has left the company but worked as a freelancer on _Gunstar Super Heroes_ and _Sin and Punishment: Star Successor_.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:3-13)
*   [Hiroshi Iuchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshi_Iuchi "Hiroshi Iuchi") – Director for _Radiant Silvergun_, _Ikaruga_, and _Gradius V_[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:3-13)
*   Mitsuru Yaida – Programmer for the _Bangai-O_ games[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:3-13)
*   Koichi Kimura - Director and Artist for _Dynamite Headdy_, _McDonald's Treasure Land Adventure_, _Stretch Panic_, and _Wario World_
*   Tetsuhiko Kikuchi – Frequent artist and character designer. Led development of _Yu Yu Hakusho Makyō Tōitsusen_, _Guardian Heroes_, _Rakugaki Showtime_ and _Tiny Toon Adventures: Defenders of the Universe_.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:3-13)
*   Norio Hanzawa – Frequent composer[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:3-13)
*   Yasushi Suzuki – Artist for _Radiant Silvergun_, _Sin and Punishment_, and _Ikaruga_[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:3-13)

Treasure places emphasis on creating original games in the action, platform, and shooter genres.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:0-3)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:3-13) They do not have a preference on gaming platforms or 2D vs. 3D gameplay, preferring to choose the most suitable depending on the game they are designing.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:8-11) The company has never viewed sales as much of a concern. They would prefer making the games they want to make, and not what will more likely sell well.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:6-8)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:7-24) Maegawa has preferred to always keep the company small to keep an "independent-minded" mentality, and help the developers' personalities shine through their games.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:7-24)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:6-8)

They expressed disinterest in sequels early in their history, but became more open to it later.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:0-3)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:8-11) They pride themselves in creating original ideas and avoiding imitating other works or being associated with games already on the market.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:2-10)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:7-24) They have made games based on licensed properties to generate revenue to pursue original projects.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:1-9)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:3-13) Explaining the Treasure design philosophy, Maegawa said it "simply, to create the games we want to make"[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:3-13) and "creating the things we love in the way we like."[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-works4-2) The company has generally employed around 20 to 30 people at any given time.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:1-9)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:7-24)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:9-25)

## Reputation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Treasure_(company)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Reputation")]

Treasure was one of the most celebrated developers of the 16-bit era and grew a [cult following](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult_following "Cult following") during the period.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:10-18)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:9-25)_USgamer_ called them "one of Japan's pioneering [indie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indie_game "Indie game") developers" and explained the "sense of integrity" in their 1990s work that was not seen in other games of the era.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-28)_Maximum: The Video Game Magazine_ called it "one of the most respected programming houses in the world" in 1996.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:2-10)_Gamers' Republic_ agreed in 1998, writing: "Any action or platform gamer worth his salt recognizes Treasure as one of the finest development houses in the world."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:8-11) In 2005, _1UP.com_ called Treasure "one of Japan's most famous independent development houses [...] releasing some of the most finely crafted, creative, and offbeat action games the world has ever seen."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:1-9) Treasure did not have any large commercial successes, which influenced _Retro Gamer_ to describe their output as "critically acclaimed yet commercially unsuccessful."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:6-8) Because of the loyal fan base but low sales, prices of Treasure games such as _Rakugaki Showtime_ and _Radiant Silvergun_ have climbed on the secondary market.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:3-13)

The company established a signature style early on that became consistent across their work.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:9-25)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:3-13) Their first game, _Gunstar Heroes_, established what _1UP.com_ called Treasure's key themes: "creativity, weirdness, and a tendency toward completely absurd levels of action."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:1-9)_Wireframe_ called their style "fast, aggressive [...] featuring bold graphics and surreal dashes of humour."[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:9-25)_Retro Gamer_ wrote that they have "consistently excellent art direction"[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:3-13) and are renowned for their "action-packed" and "explosive" gameplay.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:6-8) They explained that Treasure is "at the very cutting edge of artistic freedom, forging its own very particular path and creating a softography guided by nothing other than the whims of the creators."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:3-13) The company is known for taking risks within established genres, borrowing conventional ideas and adding their own creative touches to create something new and innovative.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:2-10)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:9-25) They became recognized for their prowess in 2D game design,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:6-8)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:8-11)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:9-25) with _Gamers' Republic_ calling their output "the finest 2D platform games on the planet."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:8-11) Treasure is also known for technological innovation; several of their games pushed the hardware to their limits.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masato_Maegawa#cite_note-:3-13)
